saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes: drift and performance metrics fit Performance Degradation Detection Test and Monitoring Signal Architecture; rollout, shadowing, rollback, fallbacks, runbooks, versioning, human review, reward hacking, chain-of-thought limitations, telemetry storage, offline evaluation, fine-tuning, and policy adaptation are also represented. However, several relevant architectural axes are not captured. First, safety can be encoded as soft reward penalties or blended scores versus explicit expected-cost CMDP constraints and safety thresholds; existing reward/objective and runtime-guardrail dimensions do not distinguish this training-time constraint formulation from runtime action restriction. Second, the taxonomy lacks policy-serving topology and capacity decisions, including API/microservice boundaries, autoscaling, and consolidation of multiple policies behind a shared endpoint. Third, it lacks monitoring coverage granularity: aggregate monitoring versus layer-specific or tool-conditioned slices. Fourth, it does not capture evaluator architecture, especially whether evaluator and acting agent share a model and how much interaction history or context they receive. Finally, it lacks a data-admission or quarantine decision for production feedback, such as approving logs for retraining or freezing ingestion during an incident. These are consequential design choices for post-deployment RL monitoring and cannot be added to existing dimensions without conflating distinct axes.

The minibatch is largely covered: safety filtering and shields fit Runtime Safety Safeguard; candidate comparison and canary/A-B release fit Validation Exposure Strategy; model rollback, retraining, fine-tuning, retrieval, feedback, drift signals, reward-hacking detection, and serving/autoscaling fit existing dimensions. However, two architectural axes are not adequately represented. First, Production Recovery Action distinguishes automated from manual rollback but does not capture the implementation mechanism for switching versions, such as traffic shifting, registry-pointer changes, configuration changes, or feature flags. Second, the taxonomy lacks a decision dimension for monitoring resolution and computation strategy: aggregate versus slice- or interaction-mode monitoring, cross-worker aggregation, rolling/percentile windows, and fixed monitoring cadence. These choices materially affect the observability of localized or tail failures and cannot be represented solely as detection tests or signal types without conflating distinct axes.

saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers most codes: reward misspecification and hacking are represented by Objective Specification, Alignment Evaluation, Runtime Safety Safeguard, and Performance Degradation Detection; offline learning, robustness, feedback-driven adaptation, logging, drift detection, shadow/canary rollout, rollback, and evaluator-source choices are also subsumed by existing dimensions. However, several concepts introduce distinct architectural axes. Serving architecture does not capture request-level admission and access controls such as rate limiting or authentication/authorization, nor the upstream stream-processing architecture that constructs the agent state. The evaluator-feedback dimension captures evaluator roles and context but not reward-model construction choices such as ensembles, information bottlenecks, separate quality/length heads, or debiased comparison-data design. Finally, logging and behavioral monitoring capture observations of reward or environment behavior, but no existing dimension explicitly covers runtime integrity monitoring of the reward implementation and of the environmental inputs supplied to it.

Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: reward design and proxy misalignment fit Objective Specification and Alignment Evaluation; evaluator configuration, human escalation, and calibration fit Evaluator Feedback Configuration and Behavioral Oversight Signals; trajectory storage, provenance, feature validation, and experiment reproducibility fit Production Evidence Capture and Evidence Provenance and Validation; monitoring signals and alerting fit Performance Degradation Detection Test and Drift Monitoring Signals; and rollback, canary, shadow, and deployment integration fit Validation Exposure Strategy, Production Recovery Trigger, Production Recovery Action, and Policy Serving Architecture. However, Policy promotion governance represents a distinct architectural decision about who or what authorizes a candidate policy to advance between lifecycle stages, including promotion rules enforced by a model registry. This is not equivalent to the evaluation method or exposure strategy: those determine how evidence is gathered, whereas governance determines how that evidence is converted into an approval or promotion decision. The taxonomy therefore has a clear gap for a policy-promotion authorization or release-governance dimension.

saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions covering behavioral and integrity monitoring, drift signals, production evidence, policy evaluation, update strategies, recovery, safety controls, evaluator calibration, and training infrastructure. However, two relevant architectural decisions remain insufficiently represented. “Offline rather than online monitoring coverage” concerns whether monitoring is executed only through offline experiment/evaluation infrastructure or continuously against live production behavior; the existing evaluation and evidence dimensions do not explicitly capture this monitoring-execution modality. “In-loop monitoring” concerns whether detection and recovery are embedded inside the RL training/control loop or implemented as a separate operational subsystem. Existing dimensions cover monitoring signals and monitoring–deployment integration, but not this distinct architectural placement decision.

All relevant open codes are subsumed by existing taxonomy dimensions. Reward specification, proxy optimization, reward hacking, and proxy–objective divergence map to Objective Specification, Alignment Evaluation, Behavioral and Integrity Monitoring, and Evaluator Calibration Method. Automated metrics, domain benchmarks, human review, LLM judges, fixed-query tests, and statistical alerts map to Behavioral Oversight Signals, Policy Evaluation Modality/Estimator, and Statistical Degradation Detection Test. Guardrails such as prompt-injection defense, restricted-topic enforcement, business-rule validation, and reward-integrity checks map to Runtime Safety Control, Inference Safety Filtering, Objective Specification, and Behavioral and Integrity Monitoring. Rollback automation, registry targets, state restoration, verification tests, notifications, and audit records are covered by Production Recovery Action, Production Recovery Trigger, Training and Deployment Infrastructure, and Evidence Provenance and Validation. Fine-tuning, online learning, replay, PEFT/adapters, evaluation gates, metric-triggered retraining, and co-adaptation map to Policy Update Strategy and Training and Deployment Infrastructure. Serving/training separation, co-location, computation reuse, and adapter serving are absorbable within the existing infrastructure and serving-topology dimensions. The remaining codes describe risks, outcomes, concrete examples, or implementation variants already represented by these axes rather than distinct architectural decisions.

uncovered_concepts: Separation of data-science and production-deployment duties
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: drift and unseen-condition risks map to Drift Monitoring Signals, Runtime Safety Control, and Deployment World Assumption; evaluation and rollout mechanisms map to Policy Evaluation Modality, Validation Exposure Strategy, and Policy Serving Topology; reward design and hacking mitigations map to Objective Specification, Alignment Evaluation, Behavioral and Integrity Monitoring, and Evaluator Calibration Method; data capture, lineage, incidents, rollback, retraining, and human feedback are also covered. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct axis for securing and governing access to monitoring, training, deployment, and policy data, including least privilege, separation of duties, and secrets management. These are relevant architectural decisions with alternatives such as centralized versus component-specific controls and automated versus operator-governed access, and they cannot be cleanly reduced to gateway authorization or evidence provenance. Role-specific monitoring dashboards likewise introduce a distinct observability-consumption decision—whether and how monitoring views are tailored to executives, on-call operators, and debuggers—that is not captured by the existing signal, trigger, or alerting dimensions.

Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: drift and OOD monitoring by Drift Monitoring Signals; reward hacking, proxy exploitation, evaluator gaming, and behavioral anomalies by Reward and Integrity Monitoring, Behavioral Anomaly and Slice Monitoring, and Alignment Evaluation; retraining, fine-tuning, replay, and continuous updates by Policy Update Strategy; rollback, fallback, checkpoint recovery, and threshold activation by Production Recovery Action and Production Recovery Trigger; and shadow validation, offline evaluation, adversarial evaluation, and human escalation by the existing evaluation and oversight dimensions. The remaining codes expose distinct architectural axes not currently represented: the breadth of production test coverage; when online updates may safely be applied; where and how often rollout-level monitoring is executed; the temporal horizon of optimization and approval feedback; and isolation/order of reference and candidate executions to prevent state contamination or evaluation exploits.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions ask distinct questions, such as production evidence capture (20) versus evidence validation (21), and recovery triggers (14) versus recovery actions (13). However, several values overlap across monitoring dimensions: statistical monitoring options such as 46.2 Tail-based importance-weight monitoring fit 24 Statistical Degradation Detection Test more directly; alerting values 24.5 Automated drift-threshold alerting and 24.10 Dataset drift index alerting should move to 9 Drift Monitoring Signals or 14 Production Recovery Trigger; and 33.4 Prometheus-Grafana monitoring stack answers deployment/monitoring infrastructure in 38 more than serving topology in 33. The broad behavioral-monitoring scopes of 10 Behavioral Oversight Signals and 45 Behavioral Anomaly and Slice Monitoring also substantially overlap; move source-oriented values such as 10.3 Human output review to the output-quality monitoring dimension 47, while retaining trace-specific values in 10.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions are phrased as clear monitoring decisions and most values have distinguishable descriptions relevant to post-deployment RL infrastructure. However, dimension 20, "Production Evidence Capture," does not fit value 20.4, "Approved production-log feedback loop"; rename the dimension and description to include feedback or move that value to an existing feedback/infrastructure dimension. Move 33.4, "Prometheus-Grafana monitoring stack," from "Policy Serving Topology" to 38, "Deployment and Operations Infrastructure," because it describes telemetry infrastructure rather than serving topology. In dimension 24, 24.1, "BFAR drift-detection test," is unexplained jargon; rename it to the existing described concept, such as "Episodic performance-degradation test." Dimension 45 contains several overly generic and overlapping values—especially 45.4, "Anomalous behavior detection," 45.6, "Continuous deployed-agent monitoring," and 45.7, "Policy behavior monitoring"—so merge or drop the redundant generic entries while retaining the more specific signals. Value 47.9, "Practice-oriented behavioral monitoring," is also vague and should be renamed to explicitly state the realistic practitioner-deployment behavior it monitors.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the main post-deployment RL monitoring decision areas with multiple candidates: evidence capture (20), provenance and validation (21), drift and statistical detection (9, 24), behavioral/reward/quality monitoring (45–47), oversight and evaluator configuration (10, 39–42), serving and operations (33, 34, 38), recovery triggers/actions (14, 13), and runtime safety controls (43, 44, 30). Each of these dimensions has several accepted, rejected, or mixed candidate decisions, including the smaller but sufficient candidate sets in 30 and 34. No major use-case area is left without a decision point; remaining issues concern taxonomy organization or semantics, which are outside this criterion.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions are strongly within scope for post-deployment RL monitoring infrastructure: 20 Production Evidence Capture, 21 Evidence Provenance and Validation, 9 Drift Monitoring Signals, 24 Statistical Degradation Detection Test, 45 Behavioral Anomaly and Slice Monitoring, 46 Reward and Integrity Monitoring, 43/44 runtime controls, and 13/14 recovery decisions all address production evidence, detection, safety, or rollback. However, 39 Evaluator-Generator Configuration, 40 Feedback Source Configuration, 41 Evaluator Calibration and Aggregation, and 42 Evaluator Escalation and Diversity primarily concern training/alignment feedback and evaluator design rather than infrastructure decisions after deployment; drop these dimensions or move only their explicitly runtime-monitoring content into 10 Behavioral Oversight Signals. 47 User and Output Quality Monitoring and 10 Behavioral Oversight Signals also contain tangential general-LLM material such as hallucination, chain-of-thought, and RLHF-style oversight; move the directly applicable production signal values into 45 or 46 and drop the remaining out-of-scope values. 33 Policy Serving Topology and 34 Serving Operational Control are relevant infrastructure decisions, though their generic serving options should be retained only where they support deployed-agent monitoring.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains several catch-all buckets, which conflicts with the requirement that each dimension represent one focused decision. Most notably, id 38 "Deployment and Operations Infrastructure" combines serving, monitoring integration, incident response, rollback, and online training; split it into focused deployment/serving and recovery/operations questions, moving values 38.4–38.8 accordingly. Id 44 "Runtime Action and Model Safety Controls" combines action limits, reward clipping, human review, simulator validity, and rule validation; split these into action/reward controls and model/environment validation, moving values 44.1–44.5. Id 45 "Behavioral Anomaly and Slice Monitoring," id 46 "Reward and Integrity Monitoring," and id 47 "User and Output Quality Monitoring" similarly bundle multiple distinct signal families; split each into focused existing-content dimensions and move their values to the corresponding question. Broad values such as 45.6 "Continuous deployed-agent monitoring" and 45.9 "Offline RL observability signals" should also be moved into the more specific dimensions they describe.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions bundle distinct decisions or contain values that are sub-topics rather than alternatives to one question. In dimension 20, values 20.4 (feedback loop), 20.7 (fallback instrumentation), and 20.8 (rollback auditing) should be moved to the existing feedback, runtime-control, and recovery/operations dimensions rather than treated as evidence-capture options. Dimension 24 mixes statistical tests with alerting and baseline policies; move values 24.5, 24.6, 24.10, and 24.11 to recovery-trigger configuration or rename/reorganize the dimension around detection and alerting. Value 33.4 is a monitoring-stack choice, not a policy-serving topology option, so move it to dimension 38. Dimension 38 itself combines integration, alerting, rollback orchestration, and training/serving topology; distribute values 38.4–38.8 to the corresponding existing recovery, trigger, serving, and monitoring dimensions and drop the emptied dimension. Dimensions 43 and 44 also bundle separate uncertainty handling, feature access, action constraints, reward controls, validation, and simulator decisions; merge or redistribute these values so each retained dimension represents one runtime-control decision.

criteria.reason: Several dimensions have at least two candidates and coherent questions, notably 14 Production Recovery Trigger, 30 Inference Safety Filtering, 40 Feedback Source Configuration, and 42 Evaluator Escalation and Diversity.
